mercy_translation.text:
What has already been said is no small proof that death has been abolished and that the Lord's cross is a trophy over it. But concerning the immortal resurrection of the body accomplished by Christ—the common Savior and true Life of all—the proof from visible facts is clearer than words for those whose inward eye is sound.

For if death has been abolished, as the argument has shown, and because of the Lord everyone tramples upon it, much more did he himself first trample it down in his own body and abolish it. And once death was put to death by him, what else had to happen but that the body should rise and be shown as the trophy over death? How could death be shown to have been abolished unless the Lord's body had risen? If this proof concerning his resurrection is not sufficient for someone, let that person at least be convinced by what has taken place before our eyes.

For if a dead person can do nothing, but his influence extends only as far as the grave and then ceases, while actions and effective works among human beings belong only to the living, let whoever wishes look and become a judge, confessing the truth from what is seen.

Since the Savior works so many things among human beings, and every day invisibly persuades such a multitude from every side—both among Greeks and among peoples called barbarian—to come over to his faith and obey his teaching, can anyone still have a doubtful mind about whether the Savior has accomplished a resurrection and Christ lives, or rather is himself Life?

Is it the work of a dead man to pierce human consciences so that people deny ancestral customs and reverence the teaching of Christ? Or how, if he is not active—as belongs to one who is dead—does he cause those who are active and living to cease from their former actions: the adulterer no longer commits adultery, the murderer no longer murders, the unjust person no longer practices greed, and the impious becomes devout?

And if he did not rise but is dead, how does he drive away, pursue, and cast down those whom unbelievers say are living gods and the demons they worship?

For wherever Christ and faith in him are named, there all idolatry is overthrown, every demonic deception is exposed, and no demon can even endure the name; merely hearing it, the demon flees away. This is not the work of one who is dead but of one who is living—and above all, of God.

Moreover, it would be ridiculous to say that the demons driven away by him and the idols being abolished are alive, while the One who drives them away, by his own power prevents them even from appearing, and is confessed by all to be the Son of God, is dead.

translator_notes: Translated directly from the Greek source.
The chapter uses the continuing moral and religious effects of Christian faith as an apologetic for the risen Christ.
Athanasius' argument reflects the polemical environment of late antiquity and should be read historically as well as theologically.
